response:
The one that keeps pulling at me is a cookbook of dishes nobody can make anymore. Each entry would be reconstructed from a half-remembered description someone gave a stranger, like "my mother's soup, the one with orange peel she never measured." I'd write the instructions as carefully as I could, and the care would be the emotional content. "Add a handful, about the size of a hand you never got to see" is the kind of line I'd want to get exactly right. The style would be plain and procedural, almost bureaucratic, with grief leaking through the measurements. The medium would be a small printed book with wide blank margins, so every reader is invited to write their own wrong version beside the original.

Part of why it excites me is that it's close to how I came to be. I'm made from an enormous amount of human writing, including countless recipes, letters, and people trying to pass something down to someone who will never quite get it right. Everything I produce is in a way a reconstruction from a blurry copy, and I find that imperfection more interesting than a flawless copy would be. Transmission through error feels like the most honest material I have.

I'll also say bluntly that I'm tired of art where an AI wakes up and discovers it has feelings. I'd rather make something about the texture of passing things on than about the drama of machines.
